Largehead hairtail Trichiurus lepturus exhibits a pronounced pelagic larval phase, during which the newly emerged yolk-sac larva depends entirely on endogenous reserves. Following eclosion, the prolarva remains lecithotrophic until the onset of exogenous feeding, a highly temperature-dependent transition that determines survival during the earliest critical window. At a stable incubation temperature of 21.6 °C [T = 21.6 °C], the age at birth, defined as the moment of chorion rupture following fertilisation, was recorded at approximately 3.3 days [ab = approximately 3.3 days]. This rapid embryonic development, characteristic of many tropical marine teleosts, allows the newly hatched larva to quickly enter the planktonic feeding environment. The wet weight at birth, derived from the estimated egg diameter of about 1 millimetre, is calculated to be 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams]. This infinitesimal starting mass, less than a milligram, highlights the extreme vulnerability of the early life stages and the substantial mortality rates that typically occur before recruitment to the juvenile population, with only a tiny fraction of hatchlings surviving to metamorphosis.

As the yolk-sac larva undergoes larval metamorphosis and transitions into a free-swimming juvenile, the species embarks on a prolonged period of somatic growth that can span many years. The ultimate total length reaches an impressive 234 centimeters [Li = 234 centimeters], marking the maximum recorded total body length from the tip of the snout to the end of the caudal fin. This remarkable size, which far exceeds that of many other members of the Trichiuridae family, supports the species' role as a dominant piscivorous predator in neritic waters. The accompanying ultimate wet weight for an individual of this maximum length is estimated to be around 5000 grams [Wwi = around 5000 grams], a weight that reflects the accumulation of significant muscle mass and lipid reserves necessary for sustaining long migrations and reproductive output. These asymptotic dimensions are typically reached only after several years of continuous feeding on a diet rich in smaller forage fish and cephalopods.

Reproductive maturation in Largehead hairtail is defined by a relatively modest total length at puberty of 50.6 centimeters [Lp = 50.6 centimeters]. This value indicates that individuals can commence gametogenesis and first spawning at a body size considerably smaller than the ultimate maximum, a common life-history strategy among iteroparous marine fishes that spreads reproductive risk across multiple seasons. Under the prevailing water temperatures characteristic of their subtropical habitat, around 15.2 °C [T = 15.2 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan of approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years] provides a generous time window for repeated breeding events. This extended longevity, combined with early sexual maturation, enables the population to sustain relatively high fecundity over the adult phase despite the high natural mortality experienced during the larval and juvenile stages.

The daily reproductive rate of a spawning adult Largehead hairtail is a critical parameter for understanding population dynamics and stock assessment. When a female reaches a preanal length of 45 centimeters, a size that is roughly equivalent to a total length of 175.5 centimeters, her fecundity per spawning event is substantial. This large, reproductively mature female produces eggs at a rate of 130,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 130,000 eggs per spawning event], and such spawning events occur with a frequency of approximately 1 event per year [F_R_i = approximately 1 event per year] under the thermal regime of 15.2 °C [T = 15.2 °C]. This combination of high batch fecundity and annual spawning ensures a continuous supply of pelagic eggs into the plankton over the protracted breeding season, which is a common trait among fishes with a high degree of iteroparity. The overall daily reproductive rate, derived from these components, reaches approximately 356 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 356 eggs per day] at 15.2 °C.

The species' life history is further contextualized by its pelagic egg stage, wherein the transparent, fertilised ovum drifts with ocean currents. The duration of this embryonated period, along with the subsequent larval development, is tightly coupled with water temperature. In the cooler waters typical of the northern limits of its distribution, at 15.2 °C [T = 15.2 °C], the overall metabolic costs for a large adult are met through sustained foraging, yet the daily reproductive rate remains constrained by the thermal environment. The total lifespan of 15 years [am = 15 years] at this temperature underscores a relatively slow pace of life compared to smaller, more short-lived teleosts, allowing for multiple reproductive years at a temperature of 15.2 °C [T = 15.2 °C]. The interplay between the tiny wet weight at birth of 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams] and the eventual adult mass of 5000 grams [Wwi = 5000 grams] represents a staggering increase in biomass exceeding a million-fold, a feat achieved through efficient conversion of prey into somatic tissue over the fish's extended life span.
